body: If you squeezed all of Earth's ozone down to sea-level pressure, the whole layer would be only about 3 mm thick, roughly two stacked coins.
The real ozone hole is healing. After the 1987 Montreal Protocol banned the chemicals causing it, the Antarctic ozone hole is expected to recover around 2066.
NASA's PhoneSat used an ordinary smartphone as its brain, and its parts cost only a few thousand dollars.
One CubeSat unit is a 10 cm cube, about the size of a Rubik's Cube.
The Apollo guidance computer had about 4 KB of working memory, far less than a single photo on your phone.
Memory foam was invented for NASA to make aircraft seats safer.
The camera sensor in most phones grew out of work at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
Infrared ear thermometers use technology NASA developed to measure the temperature of stars.
Our AI is named after Ceres. NASA's Dawn spacecraft was the first to orbit two different worlds: the asteroid Vesta, then the dwarf planet Ceres.
Some craters at the lunar south pole never see sunlight, and they are among the coldest places NASA has measured in the solar system.
With no wind or rain to erase them, the Apollo astronauts' footprints could last for millions of years.
Mirrors left by Apollo astronauts show the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Apollo astronauts left 96 bags of their own waste on the Moon.
You weigh only one-sixth as much on the Moon, which is exactly why launching from there is cheaper.
NASA's Ingenuity helicopter was planned for 5 test flights. It made 72.
The Opportunity rover was built for a 90-day mission and kept driving for nearly 15 years, until a 2018 dust storm covered its solar panels.
NASA's MOXIE made about 122 g of oxygen from Mars's air, about what a small dog breathes in 10 hours.
Sunsets on Mars are blue.
A message from Mars takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to reach us, depending on where the two planets are.
Mars's volcano Olympus Mons is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.
A day on Mars, called a sol, lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes.
